title: Rights and Provenance in AI Art
answer: Copyright and trademark, licensing, training data and opt-outs, studio security, and content credentials.

children.name: Copyright and Trademark for AI Work
children.blurb: Copyright and trademark for AI work covers the legal questions that arise when a model is trained on existing material and when its output is used commercially.

children.name: Licensing Synthetic Media
children.blurb: Licensing synthetic media covers the terms under which AI generated images, video, audio and text may be used, sold, remixed or redistributed.

children.name: Training Data and Opt-Outs
children.blurb: Training data and opt-outs covers the material used to teach generative models and the mechanisms by which creators ask to be excluded from that use.

children.name: Security for Creative Studios
children.blurb: Security for creative studios covers the protection of unreleased artwork, client files, source projects and the machines that hold them.

children.name: Watermarking and Content Credentials
children.blurb: Watermarking and content credentials cover the technical and procedural means of marking AI generated or AI edited media so that its origin can later be checked.

sections.body: Rights and provenance in AI art covers who owns what a model produces, what data went into training it, and how a viewer can tell where an image came from. In practice, studios now check model terms before a commercial job, artists register or license outputs, and platforms attach metadata to generated files. Copyright offices and courts have been asked to decide whether a purely machine generated image can be owned at all, and several have said human authorship is required. Trademark questions arise when a model reproduces a logo or a recognizable brand style. Security work sits alongside this, because a studio's own unreleased art is both a training asset and a target.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The ground is unsettled. Human authorship requirements have been affirmed in some jurisdictions, while the status of images made with substantial prompting and editing remains contested. Licensing of synthetic media is workable in contract but hard to enforce once a file is copied without its terms. Opt-out mechanisms exist for some training datasets, yet they depend on the trainer honoring them and on the artist knowing which dataset to check. Watermarking and content credentials are technically real and increasingly deployed, but they can be stripped, and no scheme is universal. Security for creative studios is the most mature area, since it borrows from ordinary trade secret and access control practice.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: Start with Copyright and Trademark for AI Work for the ownership and infringement questions that frame everything else. Licensing Synthetic Media then covers the contracts and platform terms that govern how a generated file may be used and resold. Training Data and Opt-Outs goes upstream to the datasets and the mechanisms artists use to exclude their work. Security for Creative Studios turns to protecting unreleased material and model weights from leaks and misuse. Watermarking and Content Credentials closes the loop on the viewing side, explaining how provenance is attached to a file and how far that signal can be trusted.
